item.text: {"representations":[{"case_ref":"sample_2f379fa4a808b90c","text":"During March 30–April 12, steps fell from the preceding 28-day mean of 9,552 to 6,433/day (−33%). All 13 observed days were below the baseline range, across weekdays and weekends, with no recovery; the within-window decline was small (−6.5 steps/day). April 7 movement measures were missing because wear was only 360 minutes, so continuity that day is uncertain. Other measures stayed near baseline: active minutes 53.5 versus 55.1/day, low movement 450.6 versus 447.8, sleep 469.9 versus 469.5, resting heart rate 56.3 versus 56.1 bpm, and RMSSD 45.5 versus 45.2 ms. Activity continued at 21:00 for 50–60 minutes; daytime low movement comprised ten roughly 44–47-minute bouts separated by five-minute gaps. Sleep remained around 22:50–07:00 without a meaningful weekend shift. Steps and active minutes were essentially unrelated in the window; activity versus sleep ending the following day showed only a weak negative association (r=−0.32, 12 pairs)."},{"case_ref":"sample_ee525be46f256837","text":"Against the preceding 28-day sleep baseline of 480.9 minutes/night, March 30–April 5 contained seven consecutive shorter nights: 357–368 minutes, averaging 363.4, about 117 minutes less. Sleep began at 00:32–00:43 instead of around 22:39, while waking stayed at 07:00. On April 6, sleep returned to 475 minutes and remained within the baseline range through April 12 (474–485 minutes; mean 479.9). Thus the 14-day mean of 421.6 minutes (−12%) conceals a first-week change followed by sustained recovery, across weekdays and weekends. Movement and resting heart rate remained near baseline: steps 7,979 versus 7,976/day, active minutes 54.4 versus 55.5, low movement 449.6 versus 450.0, and heart rate 56.2 versus 56.1 bpm. RMSSD averaged slightly lower, 44.2 versus 45.3 ms, with intermittent values returning to 47. Activity remained at 21:00; low movement remained ten daytime bouts with five-minute gaps. Activity versus following-day sleep was weakly associated (r=0.26). On April 6 it dropped to 357 minutes, followed by six more consecutive short nights through April 12 (359–368); this final week averaged 363.4, about 117 minutes below baseline, without recovery. Sleep onset shifted from around 22:39 to 00:32–00:43, while waking remained 07:00. The 14-day mean was 421.6 minutes (−12%); both weekdays and weekends shared the late-window change. Other measures stayed near baseline: steps 7,979 versus 7,976/day, active minutes 54.4 versus 55.5, low movement 449.6 versus 450.0, and resting heart rate 56.2 versus 56.1 bpm. RMSSD was slightly lower overall, 44.2 versus 45.3 ms, but fluctuated within the baseline 43–47 range. No measures were missing."},{"case_ref":"sample_42940b941d60f03b","text":"March 30–April 12 remained broadly stable relative to the preceding 28 days: sleep averaged 471.7 versus 470.6 minutes, steps 7,923 versus 7,938/day, resting heart rate 61.7 versus 61.8 bpm, and RMSSD 45.1 versus 44.8 ms. Active minutes rose slightly, 56.2 versus 54.7/day, while low movement fell slightly, 446.8 versus 449.7. Steps nevertheless trended downward within the window (−21.7/day), especially on weekdays, with daily values staying inside the baseline range. Sleep briefly shortened to 463–468 minutes on April 6–8, then returned to 476 on April 9; onset remained 22:42–22:57 and waking 07:00, with little weekday/weekend difference. Baseline weekends had more active minutes and less low movement than weekdays; the activity difference narrowed, and weekend low movement became slightly higher. Activity remained at 21:00; low movement comprised ten daytime bouts with five-minute gaps. RMSSD became less variable. Activity versus following-day sleep and steps versus active minutes were essentially unrelated; heart rate–RMSSD association was weak. All measures were available."}]}
